tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The compliance team avoids discussing draft findings with suppliers before the audit closes.
Several analysts enjoy to review competitor filings after market close.
The board decided postponing the bond issue until October.
Warehouse supervisors refuse to sign off unfinished stock counts.
The agency promised delivering the campaign assets by Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid takes a gerund, so "avoids discussing" is the natural pattern after this verb.

Tip: Memorise avoid + -ing as a fixed pairing; an infinitive after avoid is almost always wrong.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund, not an infinitive: "enjoy reviewing," not "enjoy to review."

Tip: Like, love, and enjoy all prefer -ing when the object is an activity.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to postpone," not a gerund.

Tip: Decide / refuse / promise / plan / hope / expect all pattern with to + base verb.

TRUE — Refuse correctly takes a to-infinitive: "refuse to sign."

Tip: If the meaning is "will not do X," expect refuse + to-infinitive.

FALSE — Promise takes a to-infinitive: "promised to deliver," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise patterns like decide and refuse — to + verb, not -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core split: avoid and enjoy need -ing, while decide, refuse, and promise need to + verb. Check each verb's fixed pattern before you judge the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The product team is considering launching a freemium tier next quarter.
Investors enjoy reading the monthly cash-flow summary.
Legal counsel decided to challenge the indemnity clause.
The courier refused accepting parcels without a signature.
Finance promised to circulate the revised budget tonight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering launching" is correct.

Tip: Consider / avoid / enjoy / finish / suggest all take -ing when followed by a verb.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading."

Tip: If enjoy is followed by an activity, use -ing, not to.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to challenge."

Tip: Decision verbs (decide, agree, refuse, promise) lean toward to + base verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs a to-infinitive: "refused to accept," not a gerund.

Tip: Swap -ing for to + verb after refuse and the sentence usually repairs itself.

TRUE — Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to circulate."

Tip: Promise + to-infinitive expresses a future commitment.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs here follow their textbook patterns correctly; only refuse is broken. Treat refuse like decide and promise — always to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The editor avoided to mention the leaked memo in the press release.
Trainee traders enjoy to practise scenario drills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource payroll processing.
The start-up decided expanding into two neighbouring markets.
The lender refused to extend the overdraft without fresh collateral.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid takes a gerund: "avoided mentioning," not "to mention."

Tip: Avoid + -ing is non-negotiable in standard business English.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoy practising," not "enjoy to practise."

Tip: British spelling "practise" (verb) is fine; the form after enjoy must still be a gerund.

FALSE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering outsourcing," not an infinitive.

Tip: Consider to + verb is a classic exam trap — rewrite with -ing.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to expand."

Tip: After decide, reach for to + base verb every time.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to extend."

Tip: When only one sentence is right, verify the refuse / decide / promise group first.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs are forced into the wrong complement. Only refuse keeps the correct to-infinitive; the others need either -ing (avoid, enjoy, consider) or to + verb (decide).

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Auditors avoid relying on verbal assurances alone.
The CEO enjoys chairing the quarterly town-hall meetings.
The committee considered delaying the product launch.
Procurement decided to renegotiate the three-year contract.
The supplier promised shipping replacements by courier overnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund works: "avoid relying."

Tip: Relying is the activity being avoided — keep it as -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys chairing."

Tip: Chairing is an activity noun-form; enjoy wants that -ing shape.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered delaying."

Tip: Consider means "think about doing," so the next verb is -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to renegotiate."

Tip: A firm decision points forward with to + base verb.

FALSE — Promise needs a to-infinitive: "promised to ship," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise + -ing is a frequent slip; force to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Gerund verbs (avoid, enjoy, consider) and decide are clean; only promise is mistyped with -ing. Swap that for to + ship and the set is solid.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The presenter stopped speaking when the fire alarm sounded.
She stopped to check the slide deck before the client call.
The analyst stopped to smoking during working hours last year.
Operations stopped updating the legacy dashboard after the migration.
He stopped asking for overtime once headcount increased.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund means the activity itself ended: he quit speaking.

Tip: Stop + -ing = cease that activity.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive means she paused in order to check the deck.

Tip: Stop + to + verb = interrupt one action so you can do another.

FALSE — "Stopped to smoking" mixes patterns; either "stopped smoking" (quit) or "stopped to smoke" (paused in order to).

Tip: Never put to immediately before an -ing form after stop.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly shows they discontinued the updates.

Tip: If the meaning is "no longer do X," use stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop + gerund again: he quit the habit of asking.

Tip: Both stop + -ing and stop + to are grammatical — the meaning decides which you need.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on stop: -ing ends an activity; to + verb means pause in order to do something. The broken item illegally stacks to with an -ing form.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Retail partners avoid stocking slow-moving SKUs before peak season.
Junior associates enjoy shadowing senior negotiators on live deals.
The board is considering appointing an interim CFO.
HR decided to freeze hiring until revenue stabilises.
The contractor refused to work without a signed purchase order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid stocking."

Tip: Stocking is the activity avoided — keep the -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy shadowing."

Tip: Enjoy always wants -ing for activities in this register.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considering appointing."

Tip: Appointing is what they are thinking about — gerund territory.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to freeze."

Tip: Freeze here is a deliberate future action after decide.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to work."

Tip: When every line looks right, still verify each verb's complement type.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences use the right complement. Confirm avoid/enjoy/consider → -ing and decide/refuse → to + verb, then mark them true.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brand promised to refund customers within five working days.
She stopped to answer a compliance question mid-presentation.
Managers avoid to schedule training during month-end close.
The committee considered rewriting the whistle-blowing policy.
He enjoys to negotiate multi-year service agreements.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to refund."

Tip: Refund is the committed future action — to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive correctly means she paused in order to answer.

Tip: Ask whether she quit answering forever ( -ing) or paused to answer (to).

FALSE — Avoid needs a gerund: "avoid scheduling," not "to schedule."

Tip: Avoid + to is almost never acceptable in exam English.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered rewriting."

Tip: Rewriting is under review — that is consider + -ing.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund: "enjoys negotiating."

Tip: Enjoy + to is a high-frequency learner error.
tasks.solution_overview: Promise and stop-to are fine, and consider is fine; avoid and enjoy are wrongly given infinitives. Repair those two with -ing.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The firm decided merging with a regional competitor.
Sales leads refuse handling refunds without manager approval.
Investors promised backing the round without further diligence.
The team avoided disclosing soft pipeline numbers externally.
She stopped typing when the video call connected.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Decide takes to + verb: "decided to merge."

Tip: Merge is a chosen next step — use the infinitive after decide.

FALSE — Refuse takes to + verb: "refuse to handle."

Tip: Refuse + -ing is not standard; rewrite with to.

FALSE — Promise takes to + verb: "promised to back."

Tip: Commitment language after promise wants an infinitive.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided disclosing."

Tip: Disclosing is the behaviour they steered clear of.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly means typing ceased.

Tip: Here the activity ended, so -ing is the right stop pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Decide, refuse, and promise are all forced into gerunds wrongly. Avoid and stop + -ing are the only correct lines.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The logistics manager stopped to inspect damaged packaging on the dock.
We stopped printing paper invoices after clients moved to e-billing.
Counsel is considering filing an injunction before Friday.
The partner decided to withdraw from the joint venture.
Interns enjoy to draft first versions of client emails.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: he paused in order to inspect.

Tip: Purpose after an interruption = stop + to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: printing as an activity was discontinued.

Tip: "No longer do X" → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering filing."

Tip: Filing is the option under review.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to withdraw."

Tip: Withdraw is the chosen next action.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund: "enjoy drafting."

Tip: Drafting is an activity — keep -ing after enjoy.
tasks.solution_overview: Both stop patterns appear correctly with different meanings. Consider and decide are fine; only enjoy is broken with an infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The agency refused releasing creative files without payment.
Founders promised to share the cap table with new angels.
Risk officers avoid escalating minor breaches to the board.
She decided cancelling the overseas roadshow.
He enjoys mentoring graduate analysts each spring.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to release."

Tip: Release is what they will not do — infinitive after refuse.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to share."

Tip: Share is the future commitment.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid escalating."

Tip: Escalating is the action they try not to take.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to cancel."

Tip: Cancel is the decision outcome — use the infinitive.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys mentoring."

Tip: Mentoring is the liked activity.
tasks.solution_overview: Refuse and decide wrongly take gerunds; promise, avoid, and enjoy follow the correct patterns.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The workshop facilitator stopped explaining when participants looked confused.
She stopped to clarify the pricing model before continuing.
Directors are considering to spin off the logistics unit.
The bank refused to waive early-repayment fees.
Staff avoid using personal devices on the shop-floor network.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund: explaining ceased.

Tip: The explaining itself stopped — that is -ing.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: she paused in order to clarify.

Tip: Purpose after a pause = to + verb.

FALSE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering spinning," not "to spin."

Tip: Consider + to is a trap; rewrite with -ing.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to waive."

Tip: Waive is the rejected action.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid using."

Tip: Using is the behaviour they steer clear of.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop appears in both correct senses. Refuse and avoid are fine; only consider is broken with an infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO promised circulating the variance report after lunch.
Buyers decided to switch to a dual-sourcing strategy.
Researchers enjoy testing prototypes with focus groups.
The union refused bargaining without an independent mediator.
Planners avoid double-booking scarce laboratory time.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to circulate."

Tip: Circulate is the pledged action — infinitive required.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to switch."

Tip: Switch is the chosen next move.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy testing."

Tip: Testing is the liked activity.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to bargain."

Tip: Bargain is what they will not do without conditions.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid double-booking."

Tip: Double-booking is the problem behaviour avoided.
tasks.solution_overview: Promise and refuse wrongly take gerunds. Decide, enjoy, and avoid are patterned correctly.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After the outage, engineers stopped to reboot the primary server.
They stopped rebooting servers manually once automation went live.
The committee considered to approve a smaller capital request.
Marketing decided postponing the influencer campaign.
Partners promised to disclose related-party transactions promptly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: they paused in order to reboot.

Tip: Reboot is the purpose of the pause.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: manual rebooting as a practice ended.

Tip: Same verb reboot, different pattern — meaning flips with form.

FALSE — Consider needs a gerund: "considered approving."

Tip: Approving is under consideration — use -ing.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to postpone."

Tip: Postpone is the decision — infinitive, not gerund.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to disclose."

Tip: Disclose is the pledged future action.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop shows both meanings cleanly with reboot. Consider and decide are inverted; promise is correct.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Store managers avoid discounting premium lines too early in the season.
She enjoys benchmarking margins against listed peers.
The board is considering spinning the payments unit into a subsidiary.
Creditors refused to accept a haircut below thirty percent.
He stopped to smoking in the loading bay after the policy change.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid discounting."

Tip: Discounting is the premature behaviour they dodge.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys benchmarking."

Tip: Benchmarking is the liked analytical activity.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering spinning."

Tip: Spinning off is the option under review.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to accept."

Tip: Accept is what they will not do on those terms.

FALSE — "Stopped to smoking" is ungrammatical; use "stopped smoking" or "stopped to smoke."

Tip: After stop, choose either -ing or to + base — never to + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Four core patterns are correct. The stop line is a hybrid error — to cannot sit before an -ing form.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The client decided to escalate the dispute to arbitration.
Vendors promised updating the API documentation weekly.
She refused signing the non-compete without legal review.
He stopped reviewing emails once the out-of-office was set.
They avoided announcing earnings before the lock-up ended.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to escalate."

Tip: Escalate is the chosen next step.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to update."

Tip: Update is the pledged recurring action.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to sign."

Tip: Sign is what she will not do yet.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: reviewing ceased.

Tip: The reviewing activity ended — -ing is right.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoided announcing."

Tip: Announcing early is what they steered clear of.
tasks.solution_overview: Decide, stop + -ing, and avoid are fine. Promise and refuse wrongly take gerunds and need infinitives.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Investors enjoy questioning management on capital allocation.
The firm is considering licensing its patents to a rival.
She stopped to question a figure in the cash-flow forecast.
They decided licensing the brand to franchise partners.
He promised to question any unexplained variance above five percent.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy questioning."

Tip: Questioning is the liked activity in the meeting.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering licensing."

Tip: Licensing is the option under review.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: she paused in order to question a figure.

Tip: Purpose mid-task = stop + to + verb.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to license."

Tip: Same lemma license/licensing — decide still wants the infinitive.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to question."

Tip: Question here is a pledged future habit.
tasks.solution_overview: Questioning and licensing recur with different governing verbs. Only decide + licensing is wrong — rewrite as decided to license.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The negotiator stopped speaking to let the interpreter catch up.
The negotiator stopped to speaking when the interpreter arrived late.
Counsel avoided to commit the firm before due diligence finished.
They refused committing capital until covenants were redrafted.
She decided to commit spare capacity to the overflow warehouse.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund: speaking paused so the interpreter could catch up; the form is grammatical.

Tip: "Stopped speaking" = ceased that talk; the to-let clause is purpose for pausing the speech, not a stop + to pattern.

FALSE — "Stopped to speaking" is ungrammatical; use "stopped speaking" or "stopped to speak."

Tip: Never combine to with an -ing form after stop.

FALSE — Avoid needs a gerund: "avoided committing."

Tip: Committing early is the risk they dodge — -ing after avoid.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to commit."

Tip: Commit is what they will not do yet.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to commit."

Tip: Commit is the chosen allocation decision.
tasks.solution_overview: Commit and speaking create denser traps. Only stop + speaking and decide to commit are clean; the other three mix complements illegally.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Analysts enjoy modelling downside scenarios before earnings calls.
The committee considered modelling a second base case overnight.
IT promised modelling the migration in a sandboxed environment.
She stopped modelling when the live feed froze.
He stopped to model a quick sensitivity before the vote.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy modelling."

Tip: Modelling is the liked analytical activity.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considered modelling."

Tip: Modelling a second case is under review.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to model."

Tip: Same surface verb modelling — promise still wants an infinitive.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: modelling ceased when the feed froze.

Tip: The modelling activity ended — -ing.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: he paused in order to model a sensitivity.

Tip: Purpose mid-meeting = stop + to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Modelling is reused under five governors. Enjoy, consider, and both stop patterns work; only promise + modelling fails.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Founders avoid pitching unfinished demos to strategic buyers.
They decided pitching the seed round only after traction metrics improved.
She refused to pitch without a signed NDA.
He promised pitching the roadmap at the next investor day.
Investors enjoy pitching follow-on ideas during office hours.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid pitching."

Tip: Pitching unfinished work is the behaviour avoided.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is the future decision — infinitive required.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is what she will not do without an NDA.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is the pledged presentation — use the infinitive.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy pitching."

Tip: Pitching ideas is the liked activity for them.
tasks.solution_overview: Pitching is held constant while governors change. Avoid, refuse, and enjoy are right; decide and promise wrongly keep the gerund.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chair stopped to summarise the key risks before the vote.
The chair stopped summarising once the board asked for a closed session.
Risk teams are considering summarising breaches in a weekly digest.
She enjoys summarising dense contracts into one-page briefs.
He decided summarising the findings without naming individuals.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: paused in order to summarise.

Tip: Purpose before the vote = to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: summarising ceased when the closed session began.

Tip: The summarising activity ended — -ing.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering summarising."

Tip: Summarising in a digest is the option under review.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys summarising."

Tip: Summarising is the liked drafting activity.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to summarise."

Tip: Summarise is the chosen reporting approach — infinitive, not gerund.
tasks.solution_overview: Summarising rides under stop (both senses), consider, and enjoy correctly. Only decide + summarising is wrong — rewrite as decided to summarise.
